ri.work: RI 2.25: midazolam 2.5–5 mg IV or 5 mg IM/IN, "may repeat PRN if the SBP >100 to a cumulative dose of 10 mg (5 mg if age ≥65)" → 10 − 5 = 5 mg remaining, gated on SBP > 100

choices.rationale: 5 − 5 = 0 mg. At age 65 and over the cumulative ceiling is 5 mg, and it has already been reached — there is no repeat available regardless of how the patient looks.

choices.text: 5 mg, if the SBP is over 100
choices.rationale: This reads RI 2.25 as allowing the full 10 mg cumulative with the SBP gate. The same protocol line sets 5 mg as the cumulative ceiling at age ≥ 65, so for a 71-year-old the gate never opens. Know both halves of that sentence.
The adult cumulative ceiling applied to a geriatric patient. The age modifier halves it, and 71 is well over the threshold.
2.5 mg is the low end of a single IV dose, not an amount remaining. The question asks what is left against a cumulative cap.

questions.work: 0.25 × 106 = 26.5 mg, over the 25 mg ceiling → push 25 mg → 25 ÷ 5 = 5 mL

ri.work: 0.25 × 106 = 26.5 mg, over RI's 20 mg first-dose maximum → push 20 mg → 20 ÷ 5 = 4 mL. RI's 25 mg figure applies only to the 0.35 mg/kg repeat

Right dose, wrong vial: 2.5 mL is 25 mg at 10 mg/mL. This question hands you 5 mg/mL, so the volume doubles.

questions.stem: One small box and one large box on ECG paper equal how many seconds?
questions.work: 5 small boxes make 1 large box: 5 × 0.04 = 0.20 s

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: At 25 mm/s each small box is 0.04 s, and five small boxes make one large box: 5 × 0.04 = 0.20 s.
The two are the right values swapped. The small box is the smaller time — a large box has to be worth more than a small one.
This counts four small boxes to a large one. There are five, which is also why three large boxes make the 0.6 s you use for rate estimates.
These are tidy numbers but not this paper. 0.04 and 0.20 come from 25 mm/s, the standard speed printed on every strip you will be handed.

questions.stem: A 6-second strip shows 8 QRS complexes. Heart rate?

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: A factor of ten out. No heart rate reaches this — the ventricles cannot depolarise faster than roughly 250–300.
The raw count reported as a rate. The complexes still have to be scaled from six seconds to sixty.
Multiplied by 6 — the length of the strip — instead of by 10. The strip is a sixth of a minute, so the count is multiplied by the number of those that fit in sixty seconds.
8 × 10 = 80/min. The 6-second method is the one that still works when the rhythm is irregular, because it averages across the whole strip.

questions.stem: Regular rhythm with 20 small boxes between R waves. Rate?

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: 1,500 ÷ 10 — ten boxes counted where there are twenty. Miscounting boxes is the usual failure of this method, which is why the 6-second count is a good cross-check.
1,500 ÷ 20 = 75/min. The 1,500 method counts small boxes between R waves and needs a regular rhythm to be valid.
The 300 numerator used with small boxes. 300 goes with large boxes, 1,500 with small ones — mixing them is a fivefold error.
300 is the numerator of the large-box method, not a rate. Here it would need dividing by the 4 large boxes that 20 small boxes make, which also gives 75.

questions.stem: Normal PR interval?

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: That is normal QRS territory. The QRS is the ventricular depolarisation; the PR measures the delay before it.
0.12–0.20 s, which is 3 to 5 small boxes. It measures the pause at the AV node that lets the atria finish emptying.
Above the normal range. A constant PR over 0.20 s with nothing dropped is a first-degree AV block.
The floor is right and the ceiling is twice where it belongs. A PR of 0.40 s is a marked first-degree block, not a normal finding.

questions.stem: Intrinsic rates of the SA node, AV junction, and ventricles?

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: The junction and the ventricles swapped. The further down the conduction system, the slower the intrinsic rate — the junction is faster than the ventricles.
Every band shifted upward. A ventricular escape at 40–60 would be read as junctional, which changes what the rhythm is telling you about where the block sits.
The first two are right. 15–20 is agonal territory — a dying rhythm rather than the intrinsic ventricular rate.
SA node 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricles 20–40. Each lower pacemaker is a slower backup, which is why an escape rhythm tells you where it came from by its rate.

questions.stem: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 with no visible P waves, abrupt onset.
questions.work: P waves hide in the T waves at fast rates; rate above 150 in this text

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: A genuine mimic and worth excluding. Flutter at 2:1 lands near 150 and shows sawtooth waves between the complexes — look there before settling on SVT.
The complexes are narrow. A narrow QRS means the impulse went down the normal conduction system, which places its origin above the ventricles.
This text caps sinus tachycardia at 150. At 190, with no visible P waves and an abrupt onset, the rhythm is above what the sinus node produces — sinus tachycardia also starts and stops gradually.
SVT. At rates this fast the P waves hide inside the preceding T waves, and the abrupt onset is characteristic. This text puts SVT at 151 and above.

questions.stem: Irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves, wavy baseline.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Irregular, but every other feature is sinus: upright P waves before each QRS, and the irregularity cycles with breathing rather than being random.
Also irregular, and the closest mimic. Flutter has organised sawtooth waves at a steady atrial rate; fibrillation has a wavy baseline with no organised atrial activity at all.
Atrial fibrillation — irregularly irregular, no P waves, wavy fibrillatory baseline. Above 100 it is called a rapid ventricular response.
Another irregular narrow-complex rhythm, but it has P waves — three or more different shapes of them. Visible P waves rule out fibrillation.

questions.stem: Sawtooth waves with 4 waves before each QRS.
questions.work: Name flutter by its conduction ratio

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Atrial flutter with 4:1 conduction. Flutter is named by its conduction ratio — four flutter waves for each QRS.
The ratio written backwards. It is stated atrial-to-ventricular, so four flutter waves per QRS is 4:1.
Sawtooth waves at a regular atrial rate are organised atrial activity. Fibrillation has none — just a wavy baseline — and it is irregularly irregular.
A counting slip. Count the flutter waves themselves between complexes, not the gaps between them.

questions.stem: Inverted P waves before a narrow QRS, PR 0.10 s, rate 50.
questions.work: Junctional P waves: inverted, buried, or after the QRS; rate 40–60

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Junctional escape rhythm. The junctional P-wave signature is inverted, buried, or after the QRS, and the intrinsic rate is 40–60.
The right origin in the wrong rate band. Accelerated junctional runs 61–100; at 50 this is a plain junctional escape.
That is defined by a PR longer than 0.20 s. This PR is 0.10 s — short, not long, which is the opposite finding.
Also slow and narrow, but its P waves are upright with a PR of at least 0.12 s. Inverted P waves with a PR of 0.10 s say the atria were depolarised backwards, from the junction.

questions.stem: Every P is conducted, PR constant at 0.28 s.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.text: Sinus rhythm with a long PR — not a block at all
choices.rationale: A PR over 0.20 s is by definition a first-degree AV block. It is benign and usually needs nothing, but it is still named.
Type II also has a constant PR, and that is what makes it tempting. The difference is that type II drops a QRS; here every P is conducted.
First-degree AV block: every P conducts, and the PR is constant at more than 0.20 s. Nothing is dropped, so it is a delay rather than a true block.
Wenckebach has a PR that lengthens beat by beat until one fails to conduct. Here the PR never changes and nothing drops.

questions.stem: PR lengthens each beat until a QRS drops, then repeats.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: In complete block the P waves and QRS complexes are entirely unrelated. Here the PR has a pattern, which means conduction is still happening.
Type II keeps the PR constant and then drops a beat without warning. The lengthening PR is what makes this type I.
Second-degree type I, Wenckebach: longer, longer, longer, drop — then the cycle resets to its shortest PR.
First-degree has a long PR that never changes and never drops a beat. Once a QRS is dropped it is second-degree.

questions.stem: PR is constant, then a QRS suddenly drops.
questions.work: Unpredictable; can progress to complete block

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Type I warns you: the PR stretches further each beat before one drops. A constant PR with a sudden dropped QRS is type II, which gives no warning and is the more dangerous of the two.
Second-degree type II. The PR never varies, then a QRS simply fails to appear. It is unpredictable and can progress to complete block.
Complete block has no relationship at all between P waves and QRS complexes. Here most P waves still conduct with a fixed PR.
In sinus arrest the P wave is missing too, because the node never fired. In type II the P arrives on time and is not conducted.

questions.stem: P waves march through at 80, wide QRS at 35, no relationship between them.
questions.work: Independent P and QRS; wide slow escape = ventricular origin

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Third-degree, complete block with a ventricular escape. P waves and QRS complexes are independent, and the wide slow escape identifies a ventricular origin.
Type II still conducts most beats with a fixed PR. Here nothing conducts — the atria and ventricles are running on separate clocks.
An idioventricular rhythm has no P waves at all. These P waves are present and marching at 80, which is what makes this a block rather than an isolated ventricular rhythm.

choices.text: Third-degree block with a junctional escape
choices.rationale: Right block, wrong escape site. A junctional escape is narrow and runs 40–60; this escape is wide at 35, which places it in ventricular tissue.

questions.stem: Every other beat is early, wide, and bizarre with no P wave.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Atrial ectopics are early too, but they are narrow and carry a P wave of their own. Wide and bizarre with no P puts the origin in the ventricle.
A couplet is two PVCs back to back. Here the ectopics are separated by a normal beat each time.
Ventricular bigeminy — a PVC every second beat. Wide, early, bizarre, and with no preceding P wave.
Trigeminy is every third beat. Count the normal beats between the ectopics: one normal beat between each PVC is bigeminy.

questions.stem: Polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline. Rhythm and national first-line drug?

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: VF has no identifiable complexes at all. Torsades has recognisable QRS complexes whose axis rotates — though if it degenerates or the patient loses their pulse, electricity is exactly right.
Monomorphic VT keeps one QRS shape throughout. The twisting of the axis around the baseline is what makes this polymorphic, and it changes the drug.
Torsades de pointes, and the national first-line drug is magnesium sulfate. It is linked to a prolonged QT.
Right rhythm, wrong drug, and dangerously so: amiodarone prolongs the QT interval, which is the very thing driving torsades. Magnesium is the answer.

questions.stem: Organized rhythm on the monitor, no pulse.
questions.answer: PEA: start CPR and give epinephrine
questions.work: Search for the Hs and Ts

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

ri.work: RI non-shockable arrest dosing

choices.text: Asystole: confirm in a second lead
choices.rationale: Asystole is the absence of electrical activity. Here there is an organised rhythm on the screen — the problem is that it is not producing a pulse.

choices.text: PEA: start CPR and give epinephrine
choices.rationale: PEA — start CPR and give epinephrine, then search for the Hs and Ts. Electrical activity without mechanical output has a cause, and finding it is the treatment.
PEA is not a shockable rhythm. A shock depolarises myocardium that is already depolarising in an organised way — the failure is mechanical, not electrical.
The question states there is no pulse. That single fact is what moves an organised rhythm into the arrest algorithm.

questions.stem: Flat line on the monitor. What do you do before calling asystole?
questions.answer: Check the patient, confirm in a second lead, check leads and gain

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Asystole is not shockable. There is no organised electrical activity for a shock to reorganise, and the pause in compressions costs perfusion.
Epinephrine is part of the algorithm, but confirming the rhythm comes first — treating fine VF as asystole withholds the defibrillation that would work.

choices.text: Confirm in the same lead at a faster paper speed
choices.rationale: Changing speed in the same lead cannot reveal activity that the vector of that lead is missing. A second, different lead is what the confirmation requires.

choices.text: Check the patient, confirm in a second lead, check leads and gain
choices.rationale: Check the patient first, then confirm in a second lead and check the leads and the gain. A disconnected lead or a gain turned down looks exactly like asystole.

questions.stem: ST elevation in II, III, aVF. Which wall, which artery, and what extra lead?
questions.answer: Inferior wall, usually the RCA; get V4R

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

ri.answer: No nitro if RV infarct; stop nitro and give fluid if BP drops
ri.work: Preload dependent

choices.rationale: The extra lead is right for the wrong reason. II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall, and the LAD supplies the anterior wall.
Wall and extra lead are right, artery is not. The inferior wall is usually RCA territory, and that is what makes right ventricular involvement likely.
All three parts belong to a different territory. Lateral is I, aVL, V5 and V6, and V7–V9 are the posterior leads.

choices.text: Inferior wall, usually the RCA; get V4R
choices.rationale: Inferior wall, usually the right coronary artery, and get a V4R to look for right ventricular involvement — which changes whether nitroglycerin is safe.

questions.stem: ST elevation in V1–V4.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

choices.rationale: The posterior wall is inferred from reciprocal depression in V1–V3, or seen directly in V7–V9. Elevation in V1–V4 is anteroseptal.
Septal and anterior wall, supplied by the left anterior descending — the widow-maker territory. V1 and V2 are septal, V3 and V4 anterior.
The inferior wall is seen in II, III and aVF, not the precordial leads.
Lateral is I, aVL, V5 and V6. V1–V4 sit over the septum and the anterior wall.

questions.stem: Stable adult SVT after vagal maneuvers. Adenosine dosing?
questions.answer: 6 mg rapid IV push with flush, then 12 mg

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

ri.work: RI starts at 12 mg

choices.rationale: This is the RI sequence, and it is what you would push here. The question asks the AHA sequence, which opens at 6 mg — carry both.

choices.text: 6 mg rapid IV push with flush, then 12 mg
choices.rationale: 6 mg rapid IV push with an immediate flush, then 12 mg if needed. The flush matters: adenosine has a half-life of seconds and has to reach the heart as a bolus.
The second dose doubles rather than repeating. A failed 6 mg is followed by 12 mg.
Pushed slowly, adenosine is metabolised before it arrives and does nothing. It goes in as fast as the line allows, followed immediately by a flush.

questions.stem: Symptomatic adult bradycardia. Atropine dose and max?

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

ri.work: RI allows starting at 0.5 mg

choices.rationale: 1 mg every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. The 1 mg dose replaced the older 0.5 mg figure in the adult bradycardia algorithm.
The previous AHA dose, superseded for adults. Doses below 0.5 mg can also produce paradoxical bradycardia.

choices.text: 1 mg every 3–5 min with no maximum
choices.rationale: The 3 mg ceiling is real. Beyond it atropine has achieved full vagal blockade, so more adds side effects without adding rate.
The RI range, which allows starting at 0.5 mg. The AHA figure is a flat 1 mg — same ceiling, different starting dose.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: Rate 60-100, regular, upright P before every QRS, PR 0.12-0.20, QRS under 0.12. The only rhythm called normal.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Identical in every respect except rate — bradycardia is below 60. Check the rate before naming any sinus rhythm.
Shares the 61–100 rate band, which is the trap. Its P waves are inverted or absent and its PR is under 0.12.
Sinus arrhythmia meets every normal criterion except regularity — the R-to-R varies with breathing. Normal sinus rhythm is regular.
Normal sinus rhythm: 60–100, regular, an upright P before every QRS, PR 0.12–0.20 and QRS under 0.12. The only rhythm called normal.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: Everything about it is sinus except the rate is under 60. Normal in athletes and in sleep; only matters if perfusion suffers.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: That is a PR finding, not a rate one. The two can coexist, but a slow rate alone does not make a block.
Sinus bradycardia — everything is sinus except that the rate is under 60. Normal in athletes and during sleep; it only matters when perfusion suffers.
Also slow and narrow, and it overlaps the same rates. The P waves settle it: sinus bradycardia keeps upright P waves with a normal PR.
Sinus arrhythmia is defined by varying R-to-R intervals rather than by a slow rate, though the two often appear together.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: 101-150, regular, upright P before every QRS. Look for the cause: pain, fever, dehydration, hemorrhage, anxiety, stimulants.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: This text splits them at 150: sinus tachycardia runs 101–150, SVT 151 and above. Visible upright P waves before each QRS also point to the sinus node.
Sinus tachycardia: 101–150, regular, with an upright P before every QRS. It is a response to something — pain, fever, dehydration, haemorrhage, anxiety, stimulants — so look for the cause.
Flutter at 2:1 lands near 150 and is a real mimic. The difference is sawtooth flutter waves rather than discrete upright P waves.
Shares the 101–150 band. Its P waves are inverted, buried or retrograde, not upright and preceding.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm, and say which rate method you would use on it.
questions.work: Sinus in every measurement, but the R-to-R varies with breathing. Because the rate is a moving target, count a 6-second strip rather than measuring one R-to-R.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Right rhythm, wrong tool. The 1,500 method measures one R-to-R and assumes the next is the same, which is exactly what an irregular rhythm does not do.
The method is right and the rhythm is not. Fibrillation has no P waves and is randomly irregular; this has upright P waves and varies with the breathing cycle.

choices.text: Sinus rhythm with PACs; use a 6-second strip
choices.rationale: PACs produce irregularity too, but as discrete early beats with odd-looking P waves, not as a gradual cyclical speeding and slowing.

Sinus arrhythmia, and the rate is counted on a 6-second strip. Every measurement is sinus, but the R-to-R varies with breathing — so a single interval would give a rate that is only true for that one beat.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: Inverted P before a narrow QRS with a PR under 0.12 marks it junctional. 61-100 makes it accelerated rather than a plain junctional rhythm.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Junctional tachycardia starts at 101. Below that and above 60, the name is accelerated junctional.
The rate band overlaps exactly, which is the trap. The inverted P wave and the PR under 0.12 are what rule out a sinus origin.
Right origin, wrong band. A plain junctional rhythm is the intrinsic 40–60; 61–100 makes it accelerated.
Accelerated junctional rhythm. An inverted P before a narrow QRS with a PR under 0.12 marks it junctional, and 61–100 makes it accelerated.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: Junctional P-wave signature at 101-150. Above 100 the junctional rhythms are called tachycardia.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Same rate band, different origin. Sinus tachycardia has upright P waves ahead of each QRS with a PR of at least 0.12.
Junctional tachycardia — the junctional P-wave signature at 101–150. Above 100, junctional rhythms take the tachycardia name.
Accelerated junctional stops at 100. Past that the same rhythm is called junctional tachycardia.
Junctional tachycardia is technically supraventricular, which makes this tempting. As a named rhythm this text reserves SVT for 151 and above with no identifiable P waves.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm. Does it meet this text's definition of junctional bradycardia?
questions.work: Junctional signature at under 40. Any rate below 60 is bradycardic, but this text reserves the name junctional bradycardia for a junctional rhythm under 40. At 40-60 it is just a junctional rhythm.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: A plain junctional rhythm is 40–60. This one is below 40, which is where this text applies the junctional bradycardia label.
Junctional bradycardia, yes. Any rate under 60 is bradycardic, but this text reserves the name for a junctional rhythm under 40 — at 40–60 it is simply a junctional rhythm.
Also slow, and also an escape. Idioventricular complexes are wide and have no P waves; a junctional QRS stays narrow.
That is the band immediately above. The rate here is below 40, which is what the question is testing.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: Wide QRS over 0.12, rate 101-250, regular R-to-R, no usable P waves. Three or more ventricular beats in a row.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Ventricular tachycardia: QRS over 0.12, rate 101–250, regular R-to-R, no usable P waves. Three or more ventricular beats in a row.
It can look the same, and getting it wrong in this direction is the expensive mistake. A regular wide-complex tachycardia is treated as VT until something proves otherwise.
Torsades is polymorphic — the QRS axis twists around the baseline. This one keeps a single consistent shape.
Identical in appearance — wide, no P waves — and separated only by rate. AIVR runs 41–100; VT does not begin until 101.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: Wide bizarre QRS with no P waves, under 40. The ventricles are the last pacemaker still firing.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Same rhythm, faster band: AIVR is 41–100. Below 40 it is a plain idioventricular rhythm.
Also an escape, also slow — but a junctional escape conducts normally through the ventricles, so its QRS is narrow.
Agonal is the same ventricular origin below 20, with complexes that widen and flatten as activity dies out. Idioventricular sits in the 20–40 intrinsic band.
Idioventricular rhythm — wide bizarre QRS complexes, no P waves, under 40. The ventricles are the last pacemaker still firing.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: Ventricular in origin and under 20. The complexes widen and flatten as electrical activity dies out.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Fine VF is chaotic with no identifiable complexes. Agonal has discrete, if dying, complexes at a countable rate.
Agonal rhythm — ventricular in origin and under 20, with complexes that widen and flatten as electrical activity dies out.
The same origin in the band above, 20–40. The distinction is rate and the progressive loss of complex shape.
Asystole has no complexes at all. Agonal complexes are few, wide and misshapen, but they are there — and that difference matters when deciding whether a rhythm is organised.

questions.stem: Wide QRS, no P waves, rate about 70. Is this ventricular tachycardia?
questions.work: Same wide ventricular look, but 41-100 is accelerated idioventricular. VT does not start until 101.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: The appearance matches but the rate does not. VT does not begin until 101; at about 70 this is accelerated idioventricular.
No — accelerated idioventricular rhythm. The same wide ventricular appearance, but 41–100 is the AIVR band. VT starts at 101.
A junctional rhythm conducts through the normal pathway and produces a narrow QRS. Wide means the impulse started in ventricular tissue.
Right family, wrong band. A plain idioventricular rhythm is under 40; the accelerated form covers 41–100.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm, including the conduction ratio.
questions.work: Sawtooth flutter waves at about 300 with every second one conducted gives a ventricular rate near 150. At that rate it is easily mistaken for SVT; look for the sawtooth between the QRS complexes.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction. Flutter waves at about 300 with every second one conducted gives a ventricular rate near 150.
Sinus tachycardia tops out at 150 in this text and shows discrete upright P waves. A sawtooth baseline is organised atrial activity at 300, not sinus.
Right rhythm, wrong ratio. At 4:1 an atrial rate near 300 would give a ventricular rate near 75, not 150.
The classic miss. Flutter at 2:1 produces a regular narrow rate near 150 that looks exactly like SVT — which is why you look for sawtooth waves between the complexes before committing.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm, including the ventricular response.
questions.answer: Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response
questions.work: No P waves, wavy fibrillatory baseline, irregularly irregular. Under 60 makes it slow rather than controlled.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular response
choices.rationale: Controlled is the 60–100 band. Below 60 the description changes to slow, which often means too much rate control rather than too little.
Also slow and narrow, but a junctional escape is regular. The irregular irregularity and the fibrillatory baseline are what place this in atrial fibrillation.

choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
choices.rationale: The opposite end. Rapid means over 100; this rhythm is under 60, which makes it slow.

choices.text: Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response
choices.rationale: Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response: no P waves, a wavy fibrillatory baseline, irregularly irregular, and under 60.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: The PR stretches further each beat until a QRS drops, then resets to its shortest. Two conducted beats for every three P waves.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: The ratio states P waves to conducted beats. Three P waves with two of them conducted is 3:2, not 3:1.
The ratio is right and the type is not. Type II holds the PR constant; here it stretches further each beat before the drop, which is the Wenckebach signature.
Second-degree type I, Wenckebach, 3:2. The PR lengthens each beat until a QRS drops, then resets to its shortest — three P waves for every two conducted beats.
Right type, miscounted ratio. Count P waves against conducted QRS complexes across one full cycle: three P waves, two conducted.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm, including the ratio.
questions.work: The PR never changes, then a QRS drops. Three P waves for every two conducted beats. The more P waves per QRS, and the more the ratio varies, the more serious the block.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Same ratio, wrong type, and the distinction is the whole question. Type I stretches the PR before dropping; here the PR is identical on every conducted beat.
Second-degree type II, 3:2. The PR never changes, then a QRS drops — three P waves for every two conducted beats. The more P waves per QRS and the more the ratio varies, the more serious the block.
The ratio reversed. It is written atrial to ventricular, so three P waves with two conducted is 3:2.
Complete block has no fixed relationship between P waves and QRS complexes at all. A constant PR on the conducted beats proves conduction is still intact.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm. Two findings.
questions.answer: Sinus bradycardia with a first-degree AV block
questions.work: Rate under 60 with upright P waves is sinus bradycardia. The PR is over 0.20 and constant with nothing dropped, which adds the first-degree block. Name both.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Sinus bradycardia with a first-degree AV block
choices.rationale: Sinus bradycardia with a first-degree AV block. Under 60 with upright P waves is the bradycardia; a PR over 0.20 s that never varies and drops nothing is the first-degree block. Name both.
Junctional rhythms have inverted, buried or retrograde P waves and a short PR. Upright P waves with a long PR are sinus with delayed conduction.
Type I requires a dropped QRS. Nothing is dropped here — every P conducts, just slowly.
Half the answer. The rate and the upright P waves make it sinus bradycardia, but a constant PR over 0.20 s adds a first-degree block that has to be named too.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm, and say where the escape is coming from.
questions.answer: Third-degree heart block with a junctional escape
questions.work: P waves and QRS complexes march independently with no relationship. The escape QRS is narrow, so it is coming from the junction rather than ventricular tissue.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Type II still conducts some beats with a fixed PR. Here no P wave conducts at all — the atria and ventricles are entirely dissociated.
The escape is correctly identified and the block is missed. Independent P waves marching through mean there is a complete block above the junction driving it.

choices.text: Third-degree heart block with a ventricular escape
choices.rationale: Right block, wrong escape site, and the QRS width is what decides it. A ventricular escape is wide and slower; this escape is narrow, so it is coming from the junction.

choices.text: Third-degree heart block with a junctional escape
choices.rationale: Third-degree block with a junctional escape. P waves and QRS complexes march independently, and the narrow escape QRS places its origin at the junction rather than in ventricular tissue.

questions.stem: Regular, narrow, rate just under 150, with P waves visible. SVT or sinus tachycardia?
questions.work: This text puts sinus tachycardia at 101-150 and SVT at 151 and above. Visible upright P waves before each QRS settle it.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Shares the rate band. Its P waves are inverted, buried or retrograde — upright and preceding points at the sinus node.
This text puts SVT at 151 and above. Just under 150, with visible upright P waves before each QRS, the rhythm is sinus — and SVT typically has no identifiable P waves.
Sinus tachycardia. This text sets sinus tachycardia at 101–150 and SVT at 151 and above, and the visible upright P waves before each QRS settle it.
A real mimic at this rate, and worth excluding. Flutter shows sawtooth waves at about 300 rather than discrete upright P waves.

questions.stem: Wide QRS, no P waves, regular, rate 150. What is this and what should you assume?
questions.answer: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia; assume VT until proven otherwise
questions.work: A regular wide-complex tachycardia is VT until something proves otherwise. Treating it as SVT with aberrancy and being wrong is the costlier mistake.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia; assume VT until proven otherwise
choices.rationale: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia — and assume VT until something proves otherwise. Treating it as SVT with aberrancy and being wrong is by far the costlier mistake.

choices.text: SVT with aberrant conduction; treat it as SVT
choices.rationale: The assumption that runs the wrong way. Aberrant SVT does exist, but betting on it means giving an AV-nodal blocker to a patient in VT, which can collapse them.
Torsades is polymorphic — the axis twists around the baseline. A regular, single-morphology wide-complex tachycardia is monomorphic VT.
AIVR shares the wide, P-wave-free appearance but tops out at 100. At 150 this is in the VT band.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm. What does the wave amplitude tell you?
questions.answer: Coarse ventricular fibrillation; taller waves mean more cells still responding
questions.work: Many ventricular sites firing at once, so nothing depolarizes in an organized way: no P waves, no QRS, no measurable rate, no pulse. Coarse VF has higher amplitude and more viable myocardium. CPR and defibrillation immediately.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Coarse ventricular fibrillation; taller waves mean more cells still responding
choices.rationale: Coarse ventricular fibrillation, and taller waves mean more cells are still responding. Many ventricular sites fire at once so nothing depolarises in an organised way — no P waves, no QRS, no measurable rate, no pulse. CPR and defibrillation immediately.

choices.text: Coarse ventricular fibrillation; amplitude tells you nothing useful
choices.rationale: The rhythm is right and the inference is wrong. Amplitude reflects how much viable myocardium remains, which is why fine VF tends to appear later in an arrest.
Polymorphic VT still has identifiable QRS complexes, however variable. Fibrillation has none at all and no measurable rate.

choices.text: Fine ventricular fibrillation; taller waves mean a longer downtime
choices.rationale: Both halves reversed. Tall, coarse waves mean more myocardium is still responding, which generally means a shorter downtime and better odds from a shock.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm.
questions.work: The atria are depolarizing normally but the ventricles are doing nothing: atrial rate 60-100, ventricular rate zero, no pulse. Can follow third-degree block, massive MI, or ventricular rupture.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Third-degree block with a ventricular escape
choices.rationale: Complete block with an escape still produces QRS complexes, just dissociated ones. In standstill there is no escape at all — that is what makes it an arrest rhythm.
PEA is an organised rhythm with QRS complexes that produce no pulse. Here the ventricles are not depolarising, so there is no ventricular complex to be pulseless.
Asystole has no electrical activity anywhere. Here the atria are depolarising normally at 60–100 — the P waves are present and regular, and only the ventricular response is missing.
Ventricular standstill. The atria depolarise normally at 60–100, the ventricular rate is zero, and there is no pulse. It can follow third-degree block, a massive MI, or ventricular rupture.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm, and say what it suggests about how long the patient has been down.
questions.answer: Fine ventricular fibrillation; lower amplitude suggests a longer downtime
questions.work: Same chaotic, complex-free trace as coarse VF but with much lower amplitude, meaning fewer cells are still able to respond. It tends to appear later in an arrest. Treatment does not change: CPR and defibrillation. Do not mistake the low amplitude for asystole — check a second lead and the gain.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Agonal complexes are discrete, wide and countable, however misshapen. Fine VF is chaotic with no identifiable complexes at all.

The misread this question exists to prevent. Fine VF is low-amplitude and chaotic and can look flat — which is why you check a second lead and the gain. Calling it asystole withholds the defibrillation that would work.

choices.text: Fine ventricular fibrillation; lower amplitude suggests a longer downtime
choices.rationale: Fine ventricular fibrillation, and the lower amplitude suggests a longer downtime — fewer cells are still able to respond. Treatment does not change: CPR and defibrillation.

choices.text: Coarse VF; lower amplitude means a shorter downtime
choices.rationale: The inference is backwards and the label does not match. Lower amplitude means less viable myocardium, which goes with more time down, not less.

questions.stem: A PVC lands on the T wave of the previous complex. What is that called and why does it matter?
questions.answer: R-on-T phenomenon; it can trigger VT or VF
questions.work: The T wave is the vulnerable period of repolarization, when some cells can be restimulated and others cannot. A stimulus there can tip the rhythm into VT or VF.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: R-on-T phenomenon; benign when it occurs in isolation
choices.rationale: The name is right and the significance is inverted. A single R-on-T is one of the recognised triggers for ventricular fibrillation — it is on the list of dangerous PVC findings precisely because one can be enough.

choices.text: R-on-T phenomenon; it can trigger VT or VF
choices.rationale: The R-on-T phenomenon, and it can trigger VT or VF. The T wave is the vulnerable period of repolarisation, when some cells can be restimulated and others cannot — a stimulus landing there can tip the rhythm.
That describes the gap after an ectopic beat, not where the beat lands. Both are measured around a PVC, and they answer different questions.
A fusion beat is one complex formed by two impulses arriving together, giving a hybrid shape. R-on-T is about timing relative to the previous T wave.

questions.stem: Name the PVC findings that make them dangerous.
questions.answer: More than six a minute, multifocal, couplets, runs of VT, R-on-T, or a patient who is unstable
questions.work: Isolated unifocal PVCs in a stable patient usually need nothing. Those six findings mark enough ventricular irritability to warn of a lethal rhythm.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.rationale: Isolated unifocal PVCs in a stable patient are common and usually need nothing. What matters is frequency, variety, grouping, timing and how the patient looks.

choices.text: More than six a minute, multifocal, couplets, runs of VT, R-on-T, or a patient who is unstable
choices.rationale: More than six a minute, multifocal, couplets, runs of VT, R-on-T, or an unstable patient. Those six findings mark enough ventricular irritability to warn of a lethal rhythm.

choices.text: Only runs of three or more in a row
choices.rationale: Runs are on the list — three or more in a row is VT by definition. They are one of six findings, not the whole of it.

choices.text: More than three a minute, or any unifocal PVC
choices.rationale: The threshold is more than six a minute, and unifocal PVCs are the reassuring kind. Multifocal ones indicate several irritable sites, which is the worrying pattern.

questions.stem: A premature complex is followed by a pause. How do you tell a compensatory pause from a noncompensatory one, and what does each mean?
questions.answer: Measure R-to-R around the early beat: at least 2x the underlying R-to-R is compensatory, under 2x is noncompensatory
questions.work: Measure from the R before the early beat to the R after it. Compensatory means the SA node ignored the interruption and kept its own schedule. Noncompensatory means the SA node reset itself, which suggests increased irritability.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Measure R-to-R around the early beat: at least 2x the underlying R-to-R is compensatory, under 2x is noncompensatory
choices.rationale: Measure R-to-R around the early beat — from the R before it to the R after. At least 2× the underlying interval is compensatory, meaning the SA node ignored the interruption. Under 2× is noncompensatory, meaning the node reset itself, which suggests increased irritability.

choices.text: Compare the PR interval before and after the early beat
choices.rationale: The PR is not what is being tested. The pause is a timing measurement across the ectopic, made R wave to R wave.

choices.text: Measure from the early beat forward to the next normal beat
choices.rationale: Measuring only forward misses the point. The interval has to span the early beat — before it to after it — to compare against two underlying cycles.

choices.text: Under 2× the underlying R-to-R is compensatory; at least 2× is noncompensatory
choices.rationale: The two definitions swapped. A full compensatory pause means the SA node kept its own schedule, so the interval spanning the early beat equals two normal cycles.

questions.stem: Name the three ECG findings of Wolff-Parkinson-White.
questions.answer: PR under 0.12 s, QRS often over 0.12 s, and a delta wave
questions.work: The bundle of Kent bypasses the AV node, so the normal delay never happens and the PR is short. The delta wave is the slurred upstroke where the ventricle depolarized early through the accessory path.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: PR under 0.12 s, QRS under 0.12 s, and a delta wave
choices.rationale: The short PR and the delta wave are right, but the QRS widens. Pre-excitation starts ventricular depolarisation outside the normal conduction system, which takes longer.

choices.text: A short PR, a wide QRS, and a U wave
choices.rationale: Two of three. A U wave is a separate deflection after the T wave, associated with hypokalaemia — not the slurred upstroke of pre-excitation.

choices.text: PR over 0.20 s, QRS over 0.12 s, and a delta wave
choices.rationale: The PR is backwards. The accessory pathway bypasses the AV node, so the normal delay never happens and the PR comes out short — under 0.12 s.

choices.text: PR under 0.12 s, QRS often over 0.12 s, and a delta wave
choices.rationale: PR under 0.12 s, QRS often over 0.12 s, and a delta wave. The bundle of Kent bypasses the AV node so the delay never happens, and the delta wave is the slurred upstroke where the ventricle depolarised early through the accessory path.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an escape beat and a premature beat?
questions.answer: An escape beat is late and rescues a gap; a premature beat is early and signals irritability
questions.work: A premature beat is an irritable site jumping ahead of schedule. An escape beat is a backup site firing after the expected beat failed to arrive, which is protective. The complex that ends a sinus arrest is an escape beat.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Escape beats are always ventricular in origin
choices.rationale: Escape beats come from whichever backup pacemaker fires first — commonly the junction, which produces a narrow QRS. Ventricular escape is the slower fallback below that.

choices.text: An escape beat is early and signals irritability; a premature beat is late and rescues a gap
choices.rationale: The two definitions swapped. The words themselves carry it: premature means early, and escape means a backup site stepping in after the expected beat failed to arrive.

choices.text: An escape beat is late and rescues a gap; a premature beat is early and signals irritability
choices.rationale: An escape beat is late and rescues a gap; a premature beat is early and signals irritability. The complex that ends a sinus arrest is an escape beat — protective rather than worrying.

choices.text: Both are early; they differ only in their site of origin
choices.rationale: Timing is the whole distinction. Origin matters for naming them junctional or ventricular, but early versus late is what separates escape from premature.

questions.stem: A pause appears on a sinus strip. How do you tell sinus exit block from sinus arrest?
questions.answer: Measure the pause: exit block divides evenly into two or more full cycles, arrest does not
questions.work: In exit block the SA node fired on time but the impulse was blocked, so the underlying rhythm stays on schedule and the pause equals exactly two or more cycles. In sinus arrest the node never fired, so the pause does not divide evenly and runs longer.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Measure the pause: exit block divides evenly into two or more full cycles, arrest does not
choices.rationale: Measure the pause. In exit block the SA node fired on time but the impulse was blocked, so the underlying rhythm stays on schedule and the pause equals exactly two or more full cycles. In sinus arrest the node never fired, so the pause does not divide evenly and tends to run longer.

choices.text: Sinus arrest divides evenly into full cycles; exit block does not
choices.rationale: Reversed. Exit block keeps the node on its own schedule, which is exactly why the pause comes out as a whole-number multiple of the underlying cycle.

choices.text: Count the P waves hidden inside the pause
choices.rationale: Neither produces a visible P wave in the pause — in exit block the impulse never reaches the atria, and in arrest it was never generated. The measurement is what distinguishes them.

choices.text: Compare the PR interval before and after the pause
choices.rationale: The PR is a conduction measurement below the node. Both of these are failures at or above the SA node, so the PR is unchanged either side.

questions.stem: Atrial flutter with a 4:1 ratio and a ventricular rate of 70. What is the atrial rate, and name the other way to get it.
questions.answer: 280; or count flutter waves in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10
questions.work: Multiply the ratio by the ventricular rate: 4 x 70 = 280. That shortcut only works when the ratio is constant, so for a variable ratio count F waves on a 6-second strip instead.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: 280; or count flutter waves in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10
choices.rationale: 280. Multiply the ratio by the ventricular rate: 4 × 70 = 280. That shortcut only holds when the ratio is constant, so for a variable ratio count the F waves on a 6-second strip and multiply by 10.

choices.text: 17.5; divide the ventricular rate by the ratio
choices.rationale: Dividing where the relationship multiplies. The atria are firing faster than the ventricles, so the atrial rate has to be the larger number.
Flutter typically runs about 250–350, and 300 is the usual figure quoted. This strip gives you the data to calculate the actual rate, which is 280.

choices.text: 280; or multiply the ventricular rate by 10
choices.rationale: The atrial rate is right and the alternative method is garbled. The 6-second shortcut counts flutter waves on the strip and multiplies those by 10 — not the ventricular rate.

questions.stem: A junctional complex can put the P wave in three places. Name them and what each tells you.
questions.answer: Inverted before the QRS (high junction), buried in the QRS (mid), inverted after the QRS (low)
questions.work: The impulse travels backward to the atria, so where it starts decides when the atria depolarize relative to the ventricles. High gives an inverted P with a short PR, mid gives simultaneous depolarization and no visible P, low gives a retrograde P after the QRS.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

choices.text: Inverted before the QRS (low), buried (mid), inverted after the QRS (high)
choices.rationale: High and low swapped. The higher in the junction the impulse starts, the sooner it reaches the atria — so the P wave appears before the QRS, not after it.

choices.text: Before, during or after — the position carries no information
choices.rationale: The position is the information. It locates the origin within the junction, which is the entire reason the three variants are taught separately.

choices.text: Inverted before the QRS (high junction), buried in the QRS (mid), inverted after the QRS (low)
choices.rationale: Inverted before the QRS means a high junctional origin; buried in the QRS means mid; inverted after the QRS means low. The impulse travels backward to the atria, so where it starts decides when the atria depolarise relative to the ventricles.

choices.text: Upright before the QRS, buried in the QRS, upright after the QRS
choices.rationale: The positions are right and the polarity is not. Junctional P waves are inverted because the atria are depolarised backwards — an upright P means a sinus origin.

questions.stem: Infant CPR: compression depth and hand technique (2025)?
questions.answer: About 1.5 in (⅓ AP diameter); heel of 1 hand or 2-thumb encircling

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

choices.text: About 1.5 in (⅓ AP diameter); two-finger technique
choices.rationale: The depth is right and the technique is the one 2025 dropped. Two-thumb encircling produces better pressures and less rescuer fatigue.
Too shallow as well as the retired technique. Under-compressing generates no useful coronary perfusion pressure at all.
The adult figure applied to an infant. Depth in a child is set as a proportion of the chest — about a third of the front-to-back diameter — not as a fixed adult number.

choices.text: About 1.5 in (⅓ AP diameter); heel of 1 hand or 2-thumb encircling
choices.rationale: About 1.5 in, roughly a third of the anteroposterior diameter, using the heel of one hand or the two-thumb encircling technique. The two-finger technique was removed in 2025.

questions.stem: Two rescuers, child, no advanced airway. Compression-to-ventilation ratio?
questions.work: 30:2 for a single rescuer or after puberty

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

ri.work: RI emphasizes continuous compressions

choices.rationale: A retired ratio from earlier guidelines. It has not been current for well over a decade.
15:2 for two rescuers on a child. It goes to 30:2 for a single rescuer, or once the patient has reached puberty.
Right for one rescuer, or for an adult. With two rescuers on a child the ventilation share increases, because paediatric arrest is far more often respiratory in origin.
RI prioritises continuous compressions and that is what you would do here. The question asks the national ratio, which is 15:2 — both are worth carrying.

questions.stem: Conscious 4-year-old, severe choking. What do you do (2025)?
questions.answer: Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

ri.work: RI 7.02 has not added back blows for children

choices.rationale: This is RI 7.02, which has not added back blows for children. The 2025 national guidance did, and the question asks for that — a real divergence rather than a mistake.
The infant sequence. Chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts below one year because an infant’s liver sits low and unprotected.

choices.text: Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
choices.rationale: Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts — new for children in 2025. Previously it was abdominal thrusts alone.

choices.text: A blind finger sweep, then abdominal thrusts
choices.rationale: Blind finger sweeps are never done. They push the obstruction deeper and can injure the airway; you remove only what you can see.

questions.answer: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts (heel of hand), repeat
