choices.text: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts (heel of hand), repeat
choices.rationale: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of the hand, repeated. Never abdominal thrusts in an infant.
The right two manoeuvres in the wrong order. Back blows come first, using gravity with the infant head-down along the forearm.

choices.text: Abdominal thrusts only, as for an adult
choices.rationale: Both wrong for this patient: abdominal thrusts are contraindicated in infants, and back blows are part of the sequence at every paediatric age.
Abdominal thrusts are never used in an infant. The liver is large and poorly protected by the rib cage, so the thrusts go on the chest.

questions.stem: Rescue breathing rate for a child with a pulse who isn't breathing adequately?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

choices.rationale: Close to the old adult figure and still far too slow for a child.
Too fast. Beyond about 30 a minute you stack breaths, raise intrathoracic pressure and reduce venous return — which costs the output you are trying to support.
The adult rate. Children have higher metabolic demand and smaller reserves, so rescue breathing runs two to three times faster.
1 breath every 2–3 seconds, which is 20–30 per minute. Reassess the pulse every 2 minutes.

questions.stem: AED for a 5-year-old, but no pediatric attenuator. Use it?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

choices.text: Only if the child is over 8 years old
choices.rationale: The 8-year threshold is the old guidance for when attenuation stops being preferred. It was never a rule against shocking younger children.
Yes — use the adult AED. A shock beats no shock. The attenuator reduces the energy if it is available, but its absence is never a reason to withhold defibrillation.

choices.text: No — wait for a unit with a paediatric attenuator
choices.rationale: Waiting is the one choice guaranteed not to work. Defibrillation delay costs survival by the minute, and an unattenuated shock is far better than none.

choices.text: Yes, but reduce the energy manually first
choices.rationale: An AED does not offer manual energy selection — that is a manual defibrillator. The AED delivers its programmed energy.

questions.stem: 18 kg child in VF. First and second shock energy?
questions.work: 2 J/kg then 4 J/kg; max 10 J/kg or adult dose

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

choices.rationale: This runs 1 J/kg then 2 J/kg — half the correct energies. Paediatric defibrillation starts at 2 J/kg.
36 J, then 72 J — 2 J/kg followed by 4 J/kg on an 18 kg child. The ceiling is 10 J/kg or the adult dose, whichever comes first.
Double throughout: 4 J/kg then 8 J/kg. The second figure is within the 10 J/kg ceiling, but the first shock is twice what it should be.
The first shock is right and the escalation is missing. Subsequent shocks step up to 4 J/kg.

questions.stem: 16 kg child in asystole. Epinephrine dose and volume (0.1 mg/mL)?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

choices.rationale: 0.16 mg in 1.6 mL. 0.01 mg/kg on a 16 kg child, from a 0.1 mg/mL concentration, repeated every 3–5 minutes to a 1 mg maximum.
Right dose, wrong strength: 0.16 mL would be 0.16 mg only from a 1 mg/mL vial. Arrest epinephrine here is 0.1 mg/mL, so the volume is ten times larger.
A decimal place out on the dose. 0.001 mg/kg is not a dose used anywhere in resuscitation.
Ten times over, and well past the 1 mg maximum as well. 0.01 mg/kg on 16 kg is 0.16 mg.

questions.stem: 20 kg child in refractory VF. Amiodarone dose?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

choices.rationale: This is 1 mg/kg. The paediatric amiodarone figure in arrest is 5 mg/kg.
Double, from using 10 mg/kg. That rate belongs to no amiodarone protocol.
The adult first dose, which is also the paediatric ceiling. On a 20 kg child the weight-based figure is far below it, and the cap never comes into play.
100 mg — 5 mg/kg on 20 kg, with a 300 mg maximum for the first dose.

questions.stem: 50 kg teen in refractory VF. Amiodarone first dose?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

choices.rationale: 10 mg/kg, double the correct rate, and well past the 300 mg ceiling that should have caught it.
250 mg. 5 × 50 = 250, which sits under the 300 mg first-dose cap, so the calculated dose stands.
The cap applied when it was not reached. A maximum only binds when the calculation exceeds it — here 250 mg is the answer.
150 mg is the adult second dose in arrest and the adult dose for stable VT. It is a real number from a different line of the protocol.

questions.stem: 14 kg child in stable SVT after vagal maneuvers. Adenosine first and second doses?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

ri.answer: 2.8 mg first (0.2 mg/kg), after medical control
ri.work: RI starts at 0.2 mg/kg

choices.rationale: RI starts adenosine at 0.2 mg/kg after medical control, so 2.8 mg is the first dose here in Rhode Island. The question asks the national sequence, which opens at 0.1 mg/kg.
1.4 mg then 2.8 mg — 0.1 mg/kg to a 6 mg maximum, then 0.2 mg/kg to a 12 mg maximum. The second dose doubles the first.
The adult flat doses, and also the paediatric caps. On a 14 kg child the weight-based figures are nowhere near them.
The first dose is right and the escalation is missing. Adenosine is given as a doubling sequence because the first dose often fails.

questions.stem: 70 kg 13-year-old in SVT. Adenosine first dose?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

ri.work: 0.2 × 70 = 14 → capped at 12 mg

choices.rationale: 6 mg. 0.1 × 70 = 7 mg, which exceeds the 6 mg first-dose maximum, so the cap governs.
The RI answer: 0.2 mg/kg on 70 kg is 14 mg, capped at 12 mg. That is the first dose on a Rhode Island truck, after medical control.
Half the cap. No adenosine protocol uses 3 mg as a first dose in a patient this size.
0.1 × 70 = 7 mg is the arithmetic done correctly and the 6 mg cap ignored. At 70 kg this patient crosses the ceiling, which is why the weight was chosen.

questions.stem: 10 kg child, unstable SVT, no IV. Synchronized cardioversion energy?

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

ri.work: RI uses 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg

choices.rationale: These are defibrillation energies, 2 then 4 J/kg. Synchronised cardioversion of a perfusing rhythm starts much lower.
Ten times too low: 0.2 J/kg has no therapeutic effect and would delay the shock that works.
RI uses 1 J/kg then 2 J/kg, which gives exactly this on a 10 kg child. The national range opens lower, at 0.5–1 J/kg.
5–10 J, then 20 J — 0.5 to 1 J/kg for the first synchronised shock, then 2 J/kg. Cardioversion energies are far below defibrillation energies.

questions.stem: Infant, HR 50, poor perfusion despite good ventilation with oxygen. Next step?
questions.work: HR under 60 with poor perfusion = compressions

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

choices.text: Continue ventilation and reassess in 2 minutes
choices.rationale: Ventilation has already been given and has not worked, which is the trigger in the algorithm. Waiting another two minutes with a heart rate of 50 and poor perfusion loses the window.

Start CPR. A heart rate under 60 with poor perfusion, despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation, is a compression indication in a child — the rate alone is not enough, and neither is perfusion alone.
It comes, and it comes after compressions have started. Circulation has to be moving the drug for the drug to reach anything.
Atropine is for vagally mediated bradycardia or AV block. This bradycardia is hypoxic in origin, and it is already failing to respond to oxygen.

questions.stem: Pediatric atropine dose limits?
questions.answer: 0.02 mg/kg; min 0.1 mg, max single 0.5 mg; may repeat once
questions.work: For vagal bradycardia or AV block

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 8: Pediatric Advanced Life Support

choices.text: 0.02 mg/kg; min 0.1 mg, max single 1 mg; may repeat once
choices.rationale: The rate and the floor are right; 1 mg is the adult maximum single dose. The paediatric single-dose ceiling is 0.5 mg.

choices.text: 0.02 mg/kg; min 0.1 mg, max single 0.5 mg; may repeat once
choices.rationale: 0.02 mg/kg, with a 0.1 mg minimum and a 0.5 mg maximum single dose, repeatable once. For vagal bradycardia or AV block.
Five times the correct rate. 0.1 mg is the minimum dose, not the per-kilogram figure — the two numbers have been swapped into each other’s roles.
The floor is the point of the question. Below 0.1 mg atropine can produce paradoxical bradycardia, making a slow heart slower.

questions.stem: Adult arrest, no advanced airway. Compressions to breaths?
questions.work: With an advanced airway: 1 breath every 6 s

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

ri.answer: Continuous compressions; VF/VT gets passive O₂ for 4 cycles, then 10 breaths/min
ri.work: RI adult arrest approach

choices.rationale: 15:2 is the two-rescuer ratio for a child or infant. For an adult it is 30:2 whether one rescuer or two.
Adult arrest without an advanced airway is 30:2, one or two rescuers. Once an advanced airway is in, compressions run continuously with a breath every 6 seconds.
That is what RI 3.03A has you do, and it is what you will do on a Rhode Island truck — but the question asks the national ratio, and the NREMT wants 30:2. Worth knowing both and which is being asked.
No resuscitation ratio uses a single breath per cycle. The compression figure is right; the ventilation figure is not.

questions.verify: The 30:2 adult ratio has no verified source yet. RI’s only instance of "30:2" is in appendix 08.01.4 Cardiac Arrest — for K9 partners, alongside instructions on positioning barrel-chested dogs. The national figure belongs to AHA 2025 Part 7 (Adult Basic Life Support), whose DOI could not be confirmed on Crossref; Parts 6, 8 and 9 are already cited elsewhere in this file and Part 7 should join them once verified.

questions.stem: How soon should a chest-pain patient get a 12-lead?

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 3.02 Chest Pain — Acute Coronary Syndrome — STEMI

ri.answer: Transmit to the PCI center; scene ≤10 min if STEMI
ri.work: RI adds transmission and scene-time goal

choices.text: On arrival at the emergency department
choices.rationale: This gives up the entire advantage of a prehospital 12-lead. The point of acquiring it in the field is that the STEMI call is made before the patient reaches the door.

choices.text: After the first nitroglycerin dose, to capture the response
choices.rationale: The baseline tracing comes first. Treating before recording can mask the very ST changes the 12-lead is being acquired to find.
30 minutes is the door-to-needle target for fibrinolysis once the patient is in hospital. It is a real number on a different clock.
Within 10 minutes of patient contact, then transmit or notify so the receiving centre can act on it. The prehospital tracing is what activates a cath lab before arrival.

questions.note: RI 3.02 says to acquire a multi-lead ECG, transmit it to Medical Control, and "Limit on scene time to ≤ 10 minutes". Note that RI’s ten minutes is SCENE TIME, not time-to-12-lead — the same number measuring a different interval from the national figure this question asks for.

questions.stem: Heart failure patient, SBP 96. Give nitro?
questions.answer: No: textbook HF threshold is SBP >100

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 3.01 Acute Decompensated Heart Failure / Pulmonary Edema

ri.work: Same answer here

choices.text: Yes, provided the 12-lead shows no inferior infarct
choices.rationale: Right-sided involvement is a genuine contraindication worth checking for, but clearing it does not lift the blood-pressure floor. Both have to be satisfied.

choices.text: No: textbook HF threshold is SBP >100
choices.rationale: No. The heart-failure threshold is an SBP above 100, and 96 sits under it. Nitroglycerin drops preload, and a failing heart at the edge of its pressure has nothing left to give.
90 is a real threshold, used for chest pain in the textbook. Heart failure carries the higher bar of 100, and this question is a heart-failure one.

choices.text: No — nitroglycerin is contraindicated in heart failure
choices.rationale: The opposite is true: nitroglycerin is a mainstay in acute heart failure with pulmonary oedema. What rules it out here is the pressure, not the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Possible cardiogenic shock. Textbook BP needed before nitro?

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 3.01 Acute Decompensated Heart Failure / Pulmonary Edema

ri.work: RI cutoff is higher

choices.rationale: The textbook threshold is an SBP above 90 with a line in place. Note that RI sets its cutoff higher at 100, so the number you work to depends on which you are being asked for.
This is the RI figure, and it is the one you would work to on a Rhode Island truck. The question asks the textbook threshold, which is 90 — carry both and know which is being asked.
No protocol sets the nitroglycerin floor this high. 120 is a normal systolic, not a treatment threshold.

choices.text: No threshold applies if it is the patient’s own prescription
choices.rationale: Assisting with a prescribed medication still requires the patient to meet the criteria. A prescription says the drug is theirs, not that this pressure is safe for it.

questions.stem: Define a hypertensive emergency.
questions.answer: SBP >180, DBP ≥120, or a rapid rise, with organ symptoms

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — JNC 7 Express: The Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee on Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure

choices.text: SBP >180 or DBP ≥120 on its own
choices.rationale: Numbers alone at this level are hypertensive urgency. What makes it an emergency is organ involvement: chest pain, neurological change, visual disturbance, breathlessness.

choices.text: SBP >180, DBP ≥120, or a rapid rise, with organ symptoms
choices.rationale: An SBP above 180, a DBP of 120 or more, or a rapid rise — together with signs that an organ is being affected. Head up, IV, rapid transport.

choices.text: Any SBP above 200, symptoms or not
choices.rationale: A chronically hypertensive patient can sit above 200 and be entirely well. The organ findings are what turn a number into an emergency.
That is stage 2 hypertension — a clinic finding, not an emergency. An emergency needs far higher numbers and evidence that an organ is suffering.

questions.stem: JVD and swollen ankles without crackles suggest which heart failure?
questions.work: Fluid backs up into the body

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Biventricular failure usually shows both pictures at once. The absence of crackles is the detail that keeps this on the right side alone.

choices.text: Neither — this is more likely renal in origin
choices.rationale: Renal failure does cause oedema, but it does not raise jugular venous pressure the way a failing right ventricle does. The JVD is the discriminator.
Right-sided. The right heart fails and fluid backs up into the body — jugular distension and dependent oedema — while the lungs stay clear.
Left-sided failure backs fluid into the lungs, which is why it brings crackles and orthopnoea. Clear lungs with distended neck veins points the other way.

questions.verify: Left-sided versus right-sided heart failure. NHLBI’s heart failure page mentions both but explicitly does not say what happens in each — it never names the lungs as a site of fluid buildup. RI 3.01 lists crackles, JVD and peripheral oedema together without splitting them by side. The distinction needs its own source.

questions.stem: Tearing chest pain to the back. What quick check supports dissection?

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 18: Cardiovascular Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.text: Listening for a pericardial friction rub
choices.rationale: A rub belongs to pericarditis, which is on the differential for chest pain but is not what tearing pain radiating to the back is pointing at.

Worth acquiring, and it will not settle this. A dissection can produce a normal tracing or an inferior infarct pattern if it involves a coronary ostium — so the 12-lead neither confirms nor excludes it.

choices.text: Capillary refill in all four limbs
choices.rationale: Too blunt to catch it. Refill is affected by temperature, age and perfusion generally, whereas a pressure difference between the arms points at a specific obstruction.
Blood pressure in both arms. A dissection that involves the origin of a subclavian produces a marked difference between the two sides.

questions.verify: Checking blood pressure in both arms is standard physical examination technique. Neither JNC 7 Express nor the RI protocols describe it, and no federal source checked gives the manoeuvre or the size of difference that would support a dissection.

questions.stem: Drops per mL in a microdrip vs macrodrip set?
questions.work: Micro for small volumes and kids

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: The two sets swapped. A microdrip makes small drops, so it takes more of them to fill a millilitre — the bigger drop factor is always the micro set.
A microdrip is 60 gtt/mL, a macrodrip 10 or 15 gtt/mL. Micro is for small volumes and children, where an uncounted extra 50 mL matters.
20 gtt/mL macrodrip sets do exist, but 10 and 15 are the common ones and 30 gtt/mL is not a standard set at all. Read the factor off the tubing packet rather than assuming it.
This has the microdrip delivering fewer drops per millilitre than a macrodrip, which is backwards by definition — smaller drops mean more of them.

questions.stem: Is lactated Ringer's isotonic, hypotonic, or hypertonic? D5W?

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: True of the bag and not of the patient. D5W measures isotonic on the shelf, then the dextrose is taken up and leaves free water behind — which is why it is not a volume-replacement fluid.
Both reversed. Lactated Ringer's is built to sit close to plasma, which is what makes it a resuscitation fluid.
The D5W half is right. The hypertonic fluid on the shelf is 3% saline, not LR.
Lactated Ringer's is isotonic. D5W is isotonic in the bag, but the dextrose is metabolised almost immediately and what remains is free water, so physiologically it behaves as hypotonic.

questions.stem: Swelling and cool skin at the IV site, flow slowing. Problem and fix?
questions.answer: Infiltration: stop, remove, restart in the other extremity
questions.work: Don't restart below the bad site on the same limb

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

choices.text: Phlebitis: warm compress and continue the infusion
choices.rationale: Phlebitis is the other site complication and it looks different: warm, red and tender along the vein line. Cool and swollen points away from inflammation and toward leaked fluid.

choices.text: Infiltration: restart distal to the site on the same arm
choices.rationale: Right diagnosis, wrong site. Anything infused below the failed puncture runs back out through it, so the new line goes in the other extremity or well proximal.

choices.text: Infiltration: stop, remove, restart in the other extremity
choices.rationale: Cool, swollen and slowing is fluid going into the tissue rather than the vein. Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, and restart on the other side.

choices.text: Infiltration: slow the rate and keep the line running
choices.rationale: Correct diagnosis, wrong action. Slowing it only slows the rate at which fluid enters the tissue — and if the drug is a vesicant the damage continues either way.

questions.stem: Proximal tibia IO landmark?
questions.answer: Find the tibial tuberosity, then about 2 cm medial

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

choices.text: Mid-shaft of the tibia, on the flat anterior surface
choices.rationale: The flat surface is the right idea in the wrong place. Mid-shaft is dense cortical bone with little marrow — the proximal site is chosen for the cancellous bone behind it.

choices.text: About 2 cm lateral to the tibial tuberosity
choices.rationale: Wrong side. Lateral takes you off the flat anteromedial surface and toward the fibula, where the landmark and the bone both run out.

choices.text: Find the tibial tuberosity, then about 2 cm medial
choices.rationale: Find the tibial tuberosity and move about 2 cm medial, onto the flat part of the bone. Treat the centimetre figures as the textbook landmark — RI defers to the insertion sites in the device manufacturer’s FDA-approved instructions, so confirm against the kit you actually carry.

choices.text: About 2 cm proximal to the tibial tuberosity
choices.rationale: Going up rather than across puts the needle at or above the growth plate in a child. The movement from the tuberosity is medial, onto the flat surface.

questions.stem: Which catheter is larger, 14 or 22 gauge?

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Gauge runs backwards: the smaller the number, the larger the catheter. A 14 is the large-bore trauma line, a 22 the small one you would use on fragile veins.
This reads the number as a size. Gauge counts how many catheters fit across a fixed width, so a higher number means a narrower lumen.

choices.text: They are the same bore; the gauge number gives the length
choices.rationale: Length is a separate specification printed alongside the gauge. The gauge itself describes the bore, which is what governs flow.

choices.text: Neither — gauge describes length, so bore is read off the colour code
choices.rationale: The colour codes are real and useful — orange for 14, blue for 22 — but they encode the gauge rather than replacing it. Gauge is the bore.

questions.stem: Pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, tripod positioning, dyspnea worsening over days.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.08 Adult Respiratory Distress (Asthma/COPD/RAD)

choices.rationale: Asthma also presents with bronchospasm and prolonged expiration, but it comes on in minutes to hours and spares the chest wall. Barrel chest is years of air trapping.
Pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest and tripoding are all chronic adaptations, and the days-long course fits an exacerbation of established disease rather than a new event.
Failure also builds over days, but it brings orthopnoea, swollen legs and crackles rather than a barrel chest, and patients sit up rather than tripod.
A pneumothorax is sudden and one-sided — sharp pain and absent breath sounds on that side. Nothing here is sudden, and the chest findings are symmetrical.

questions.stem: Acute bronchospasm, mucus, and edema; wheeze on exhalation; history of asthma.
questions.work: Reversible triad: smooth-muscle spasm, mucus, edema

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.08 Adult Respiratory Distress (Asthma/COPD/RAD)

ri.answer: Albuterol 2.5-5 mg (initial dose + ipratropium 500 mcg) via SVN, up to 4 doses; methylprednisolone 125 mg IV; epinephrine 0.3 mg IM if in extremis, may repeat every 15 min x2 (med control)
ri.work: RI 2.08A adult respiratory distress ladder

choices.rationale: Anaphylaxis can present with bronchospasm and does belong on the list, but it brings urticaria, angioedema or hypotension and an exposure. None is described here.
The right picture in the wrong patient. Bronchiolitis is a first wheeze in a child under two following a cold, not an exacerbation in someone with known asthma.
Also bronchospasm with wheeze, but COPD is built on years of fixed change and a barrel chest. The stated asthma history and the fully reversible triad point the other way.
Asthma exacerbation — the reversible triad of smooth-muscle spasm, mucus and oedema. Reversibility is what separates it from COPD.

questions.stem: A "silent chest" in an asthma patient means what?
questions.work: RI 2.08A NOTES, verbatim: "A ‘silent chest’ in the asthmatic patient is a pre-respiratory arrest indicator." Airflow is too poor to make a wheeze.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.08 Adult Respiratory Distress — NOTES

choices.text: Mucus has plugged one mainstem bronchus
choices.rationale: Plugging does happen in severe asthma and would reduce sounds on one side. The silent chest is the whole chest, and it reflects global loss of airflow.

choices.text: The treatment is working and air movement has settled
choices.rationale: The most dangerous misreading in respiratory medicine. A wheeze needs airflow to make the sound — losing it means there is no longer enough air moving to produce one.
Pre-respiratory-arrest, not improvement. Airflow has fallen too far to generate a wheeze at all. This patient needs assisted ventilation now, not another nebuliser.
A pneumothorax would silence one side. A silent chest in asthma is bilateral, and it is about flow rather than air in the pleural space.

questions.stem: Patient in respiratory distress not improving after the first nebulizer treatment. Next non-drug step?
questions.work: RI 2.08A: consider CPAP for patients not responding to initial therapy

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.08 Adult Respiratory Distress / Procedure 7.01 CPAP

questions.note: RI v2026.02 gives two different pressures for this exact indication. Protocol 2.08A (Respiratory Distress — Asthma/COPD/RAD) says "consider continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) at 5-10 cmH2O". Procedure 7.01 step 6 says to titrate upward from zero to a maximum "3-5 cmH20 for asthma or COPD", reserving the higher range for pulmonary edema, near-drowning, aspiration and pneumonia. Know both numbers: 2.08A = 5-10 cmH2O, 7.01 = 3-5 cmH2O for asthma/COPD. Which one your service treats as authoritative is a question for your medical director, and it is a fair thing to ask in class. On the national exam, CPAP pressure is not tested to a RI-specific number.

choices.rationale: CPAP at 5–10 cmH2O, per RI 2.08A, for a patient not responding to initial therapy. Note that RI procedure 7.01 states 3–5 cmH2O for the same indication — the two RI documents disagree, and that is flagged in the app rather than quietly resolved.

This is RI procedure 7.01, which reserves 5–10 for pulmonary oedema, near-drowning, aspiration and pneumonia. Protocol 2.08A gives 5–10 for asthma and COPD. The two genuinely contradict each other in v2026.02 and it needs an OEMS ruling.
Beyond the AEMT scope of practice, and a step past what the question asks. CPAP is the non-invasive move that often prevents getting here.

choices.text: A second nebuliser before anything else
choices.rationale: More of a treatment that has not worked. The question asks specifically for the next non-drug step, which is positive pressure.

questions.verify: UNRESOLVED IN v2026.02 (re-checked 15 Oct 2026): 2.08A states 5-10 cmH2O for asthma/COPD/RAD; procedure 7.01 step 6 states 3-5 cmH2O for asthma or COPD and reserves 5-10 for pulmonary edema, near-drowning, aspiration or pneumonia. The two RI documents disagree for the same indication. Needs OEMS clarification — this is not a lookup failure.

questions.stem: A chronic CO2 retainer on high-flow O2 becomes drowsy with slower breathing. Why, and what do you do?
questions.answer: High O2 can blunt hypoxic drive
questions.work: Support ventilation; never withhold O2 from a patient who needs it

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.text: Oxygen toxicity has damaged the alveoli
choices.rationale: Pulmonary oxygen toxicity is real but develops over a day or more of high concentrations. It does not explain drowsiness within a single transport.

choices.text: The patient is tiring, so reduce the oxygen and observe
choices.rationale: This treats the oxygen as the enemy. The patient is hypoventilating and needs ventilatory support — removing oxygen from someone who is hypoxic kills faster than hypercapnia does.

choices.text: CO2 narcosis cannot occur while supplemental oxygen is running
choices.rationale: Backwards. The rising CO2 in this scenario is happening because of the supplemental oxygen, not in spite of it.

choices.text: High O2 can blunt hypoxic drive
choices.rationale: High-flow oxygen can blunt the hypoxic drive in a chronic retainer. Support ventilation — and never withhold oxygen from a patient who needs it. The answer is to assist breathing, not to turn the oxygen down and walk away.

questions.verify: Hypoxic drive: see resp-hypoxic-drive. No RI or federal source found.

questions.stem: Normal expiration lasts about how much longer than inspiration?
questions.work: Prolonged further in asthma, shortened in tachypnea

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: 1:1 is what you see in significant distress or with poorly set mechanical ventilation, not at rest.
An I:E of 1:3 or longer is the obstructed pattern you find in a severe asthma or COPD exacerbation — a finding, not the baseline.
Reversed. Expiration is the passive, longer phase — roughly 1:2 inspiration to expiration at rest.
About twice as long, an I:E ratio near 1:2. It lengthens further in asthma as air struggles to get out, and shortens in tachypnoea.

questions.verify: The I:E ratio of normal spontaneous breathing has no RI or federal source. RI’s only I:E figure is a ventilation instruction inside procedure 7.07 Cricothyrotomy.

questions.stem: 6 months to 6 years old, barking seal cough, stridor, gradual onset after a cold.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.08 Pediatric Respiratory Distress (Asthma/RAD/Croup)

ri.answer: For stridor at rest: nebulized epinephrine (2.25% solution 0.5 mL/3 mL NS, or 1 mg/mL 5 mg), may repeat x1; dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM/IV, max 10 mg
ri.work: RI 2.08P pediatric croup

choices.rationale: Can produce stridor, but it starts abruptly in a well child. The preceding cold and the gradual build are against it.
The one that has to be excluded, and it looks different: abrupt onset, high fever, a toxic-looking drooling child, and no barking cough. Croup builds over days after a cold.
Croup — a viral upper respiratory infection causing subglottic oedema. The barking seal cough with gradual onset after a cold is the picture.
Also viral and also follows a cold, but it obstructs the lower airway and produces wheeze. Stridor and a barking cough are upper-airway findings.

questions.stem: Toxic-appearing child, drooling, tripod position, sudden high fever, stridor. What do you avoid?
questions.answer: Epiglottitis; avoid airway manipulation and suctioning
questions.work: Let secretions drain passively; most can be bag-mask ventilated if obstruction is complete

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.08 Pediatric Respiratory Distress (Asthma/RAD/Croup)

choices.text: Epiglottitis; suction the drool to protect the airway
choices.rationale: Right diagnosis, wrong hands. Suctioning is airway manipulation, and in epiglottitis it can provoke laryngospasm and complete obstruction. Let the secretions drain.

choices.text: Epiglottitis; avoid airway manipulation and suctioning
choices.rationale: Epiglottitis — avoid airway manipulation and suctioning. Let secretions drain passively, keep the child calm and in a position of comfort. Most can still be bag-mask ventilated if the obstruction becomes complete.
That is the croup pathway, and croup is the gradual one. Sudden high fever in a toxic, drooling child is epiglottitis until proven otherwise.

choices.text: Retropharyngeal abscess; lay the child supine for transport
choices.rationale: A real differential for fever and drooling. Laying any of these children flat is wrong — it worsens obstruction, and position of comfort is the rule.

questions.stem: Under 2 years old, winter, first wheezing episode after a cold.
questions.work: Largely supportive care; nebulized epinephrine not typically helpful unless the patient is in extremis

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.08 Pediatric Respiratory Distress (Asthma/RAD/Croup)

choices.rationale: A first wheezing episode under two, in winter, after a cold, is bronchiolitis far more often than asthma. Asthma needs a pattern of recurrence to diagnose.
Same season and same viral prelude, different airway. Croup obstructs above the cords and makes stridor; this child is wheezing.
Possible, and it tends to bring fever with focal findings rather than diffuse wheeze in a well-appearing infant.
Bronchiolitis, usually RSV. Care is largely supportive; nebulised epinephrine is not typically helpful unless the child is in extremis.

questions.stem: Sudden pleuritic chest pain, unilaterally absent breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion in a tall thin young male.
questions.work: Tracheal deviation is a late sign

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Pleural Disorders — Causes and Risk Factors

choices.rationale: Spontaneous pneumothorax — the classic tall, thin young male. Tracheal deviation is a late sign and its absence does not exclude anything.
The same findings plus haemodynamic collapse: hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal shift. Nothing here says the patient is decompensating yet.
Shares the sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnoea, but breath sounds are usually present and equal, and percussion is normal. Unilateral absence plus hyperresonance is air in the pleural space.
An effusion is fluid, so it is dull to percussion. Hyperresonance means air.

questions.stem: Decreased breath sounds at one lung base, dull to percussion, patient feels better sitting up.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Pleural Disorders — Causes and Risk Factors

choices.rationale: Collapse also reduces sounds and can be dull. It tends to follow immobility or an obstructing lesion rather than producing positional relief.
Pleural effusion. Fluid at the base gives reduced sounds and dullness, and sitting up lets the fluid settle away from the upper lung. Definitive treatment is drainage.
Air is hyperresonant; this is dull. The percussion note separates the two before anything else does.
Consolidation is also dull with reduced sounds, which makes this a genuine differential — but it usually brings fever and crackles rather than relief on sitting up.

questions.stem: Sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain after a long flight or recent surgery.
questions.work: Think DVT source; causes a V/Q mismatch

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Venous Thromboembolism — Causes and Risk Factors

choices.rationale: Always on the list for chest pain, but MI pain is typically pressure rather than pleuritic, and it does not key to immobility the way this history does.
Pulmonary embolism. Think of a DVT as the source — a long flight or recent surgery is the immobility that produces one — and a V/Q mismatch as the mechanism.
Also sudden and pleuritic, but it gives unilateral absent sounds and hyperresonance, and it does not care about recent travel or surgery.
The diagnosis that gets a patient with a PE sent home. Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the risk factors in this history make exclusion impossible in the field.

questions.stem: High-pitched sound heard on inspiration from an upper-airway obstruction. Name it, and how does it differ from wheezing?
questions.work: Stridor is upper-airway and inspiratory; wheezing is lower-airway and usually expiratory

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Low-pitched and rattling, caused by secretions in the larger airways, and it usually clears or changes with a cough.
Stridor. It is upper-airway and inspiratory, where wheezing is lower-airway and usually expiratory — that pairing is the whole distinction.
Also an upper-airway noise, and a good distractor for that reason. Stertor is the low snoring sound of pharyngeal soft tissue, not the high-pitched laryngeal one.
The other one. Wheeze comes from the lower airway and is usually expiratory; stridor comes from above the cords and is heard on inspiration.

questions.verify: Stridor versus wheeze: RI uses both terms but defines neither. Needs a source for the definitions.

questions.stem: Target SpO2 range for supplemental oxygen therapy?
questions.work: RI 1.01, verbatim: with "a SpO2 of <94%, oxygen should be administered via appropriate delivery device to maintain the SpO2 in a range of 94-99%", titrated to the lowest concentration that holds it there.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 1.01 Routine Patient Care

choices.rationale: More is not better once saturation is adequate. Driving to 100% adds free-radical injury and, in a retainer, suppresses the respiratory drive.
Close, and the floor is too low. Below 94% is where tissue oxygen delivery starts falling away quickly.
A real target, used for a known chronic CO2 retainer. It is not the general figure, and applying it to everyone under-oxygenates.
94–99%. Enough to correct hypoxia without pushing to 100%, where the extra oxygen buys nothing and may do harm.

questions.stem: bG 45 mg/dL, patient awake and alert.
questions.work: Recheck bG in 15 minutes; repeat the dose if still ≤60 mg/dL

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Reserved for a patient who cannot take it by mouth. Starting a line on someone awake enough to swallow adds delay and risk for no benefit.
Glucagon is the route when there is no IV access and the patient cannot swallow safely. It is also slower, needing liver glycogen to work.

choices.text: Oral glucose 15 g PO, recheck in 60 minutes
choices.rationale: Right treatment, wrong interval. The recheck is at 15 minutes — an hour is long enough for a patient who did not respond to deteriorate unnoticed.
Awake, alert and able to protect the airway means the sugar goes in by mouth: 15 g of oral glucose, recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still at or below 60 mg/dL.

questions.stem: bG 38 mg/dL, adult, not alert to verbal stimuli, no IV access yet.
questions.answer: Glucagon 1 mg IM (or 3 mg IN Baqsimi)
questions.work: RI 2.10A: glucagon when IV access cannot be established

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: The treatment of choice once there is a line — but the question states there is no access yet. Glucagon buys the time to get one.
0.5 mg is the paediatric figure for a child under 20 kg. This is an adult, and the adult dose is 1 mg.
Not alert to verbal stimuli means the airway is not reliably protected. Glucose gel in that mouth is an aspiration risk.

choices.text: Glucagon 1 mg IM (or 3 mg IN Baqsimi)
choices.rationale: Glucagon 1 mg IM, or 3 mg intranasally, is what RI 2.10A reaches for when IV access cannot be established and the patient cannot take anything by mouth.

questions.stem: Peds hypoglycemia, no IV access. Textbook (national) glucagon dose?
questions.answer: 0.5 mg IM if under 20 kg, 1 mg IM if 20 kg or more; may repeat in 7-10 min

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

ri.work: RI dosing is weight-based, not the flat two-tier textbook dose

choices.rationale: A weight-based figure, but not one in either scheme. RI’s weight-based dose is 0.1 mg/kg; the textbook uses flat tiers.

This is RI 2.10P, which doses paediatric glucagon by weight rather than by band. The question asks the national textbook answer, which uses the two-tier flat dose — both are in use and they are not the same.
The adult dose applied to every child. The two-tier scheme exists precisely because a 10 kg toddler and a 40 kg adolescent are not the same patient.

choices.text: 0.5 mg IM if under 20 kg, 1 mg IM if 20 kg or more; may repeat in 7-10 min
choices.rationale: 0.5 mg IM under 20 kg, 1 mg IM at 20 kg or above, repeated in 7–10 minutes if needed. Two tiers split at 20 kg.

questions.stem: Adult, symptomatic hypoglycemia, IV access available. Textbook (national) dextrose dose?
questions.answer: 12.5-25 g of D50 IV push over at least 3 minutes

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

ri.answer: D10 250 mL (25 g) IV over 5 minutes; may repeat once in 5 minutes if bG <60. RI carries D10 only, no D50 on the truck.
ri.work: RI concentration differs from the textbook

choices.text: D10 250 mL (25 g) IV over 5 minutes
choices.rationale: This is what RI does, and it is what is on the truck — RI carries D10 and no D50 at all. The question asks the national textbook dose, which is written around D50.

choices.text: 12.5-25 g of D50 IV push over at least 3 minutes
choices.rationale: 12.5–25 g of D50 IV push over at least three minutes. D50 is viscous and sclerosing, which is why it goes slowly and through a confirmed line.
A full 50 mL ampoule is 25 g, not 50 g. The figure doubles the largest dose in the range.

choices.text: D25 IV push for an adult
choices.rationale: D25 is the paediatric concentration, made by diluting D50. For an adult the textbook answer is D50 and RI’s answer is D10.

questions.stem: Diabetic ketoacidosis: breath odor and respiratory pattern?
questions.work: Blowing off CO2 to compensate for the metabolic acidosis

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: The pattern is right and the odour is not. An ammonia or urine-like smell suggests uraemia from renal failure; ketoacidosis smells of acetone.
Fruity or acetone breath with Kussmaul respirations — deep and rapid. The breathing is the body blowing off CO2 to compensate for a metabolic acidosis.
Backwards. Shallow slow breathing would worsen the acidosis; the compensation drives respiration deeper and faster, and losing it is an ominous sign.
The odour is right and the pattern is not. Cheyne-Stokes cycles between deep and absent breathing and points at brainstem or severe heart failure, not acidosis.

questions.stem: bG 310 mg/dL, warm dry skin, Kussmaul respirations, signs of dehydration, no CHF history. IV fluid?
questions.answer: Normal saline 500 mL bolus, repeat as needed, then infuse at 150 mL/hr

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: A real RI figure from elsewhere — it is the sickle-cell and paediatric bolus. The hyperglycaemia row uses a flat 500 mL in an adult.
Both the fluid and the rate are off. The protocol specifies saline, and an uncontrolled litre risks overshooting in a patient whose history you do not yet have.
The glucose is already 310 mg/dL. This treats the opposite problem and would make the dehydration and osmotic diuresis worse.

choices.text: Normal saline 500 mL bolus, repeat as needed, then infuse at 150 mL/hr
choices.rationale: Normal saline 500 mL bolus, repeated as needed, then an infusion at 150 mL/hr. This is the RI 2.10A row for a blood glucose of 250 mg/dL or above.

questions.stem: Type 2 diabetic, bG 640, no ketones, lethargic, severely dehydrated.
questions.work: No ketosis distinguishes it from DKA; fluid deficit can run 10 L or more

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: It shares the dehydration and the heavy urine output, but it is a water-handling disorder and the blood glucose is normal.
The closest wrong answer. DKA is a type 1 picture with ketones and a glucose usually well under 600; here there are no ketones and the sugar is far higher.
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. The absence of ketosis is what separates it from DKA, and the fluid deficit can run to 10 litres or more.
A glucose of 640 mg/dL is the opposite end. Lethargy appears at both extremes, which is why the meter settles it rather than the presentation.

questions.stem: Sickle cell patient, severe joint/back pain, known diagnosis, no fever.
questions.work: Analgesia per the age-appropriate Patient Comfort Protocol, plus NS 20 mL/kg IV if dehydrated

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: The pulmonary form of the same crisis, and it needs the chest findings — fever, cough, chest pain, hypoxia — none of which are here.
A vaso-occlusive crisis. Analgesia per the age-appropriate Patient Comfort Protocol, plus normal saline 20 mL/kg IV if dehydrated.
Also a sickle-cell emergency, but it presents as sudden profound anaemia — pallor, breathlessness, tachycardia — rather than as pain.
Another real complication, mostly in young children, with a rapidly enlarging tender spleen and circulatory collapse. Joint and back pain is not its picture.

questions.stem: Sickle cell patient with fever, chest pain, cough, and hypoxia.
questions.work: A vaso-occlusive crisis with pulmonary involvement; also treat per respiratory distress

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: The fever, hypoxia and chest findings are exactly the pulmonary involvement that moves it out of this category.
Acute chest syndrome — a vaso-occlusive crisis with pulmonary involvement. Treat the respiratory distress alongside it.
Worth keeping on the list, since sickle-cell patients do clot. But the fever and cough point to the chest syndrome, which is far commoner in this population.
Clinically almost identical, and that is the trap. In a sickle-cell patient this combination is treated as acute chest syndrome until proven otherwise, because it deteriorates far faster.

questions.stem: Hemophilia A vs B: which clotting factor is low in each?
questions.answer: A: factor VIII (more common). B: factor IX.
questions.work: Same signs and symptoms in both

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.text: A: factor VIII (more common). B: factor IX.
choices.rationale: Haemophilia A lacks factor VIII and is the commoner of the two; haemophilia B lacks factor IX. Both present identically, which is why the distinction is a laboratory one rather than a field one.

choices.text: Both lack factor VIII, differing only in severity
choices.rationale: They do look the same in the field, which makes this tempting. The deficiency is genuinely a different protein in each.

choices.text: A: factor IX. B: factor VIII.
choices.rationale: The two swapped. A is the common one and it is factor VIII — the alphabetical order of the letters does not follow the numbering of the factors.

choices.text: A: factor VIII. B: factor XI.
choices.rationale: Factor XI deficiency is real but it is haemophilia C, a third and much rarer condition. B is factor IX.

questions.stem: History of Addison’s disease, hypotension not responding to IV fluids.
questions.work: RI 2.03: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (preferred), or methylprednisolone 125 mg IV, or dexamethasone 10 mg IV

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Also causes fluid-refractory hypotension, and also wants a steroid eventually. Without urticaria, angioedema or an exposure, the history points elsewhere.
Fluid-refractory hypotension fits sepsis too, and the two can coexist. What points here is the stated Addison’s history — in that patient the steroid is the missing piece.
Adrenal insufficiency. RI 2.03 gives hydrocortisone 100 mg IV as preferred, or methylprednisolone 125 mg IV, or dexamethasone 10 mg IV.
Worth checking, and genuinely common in adrenal crisis — but a low sugar does not explain hypotension that will not respond to fluid.

questions.stem: Which blood glucose values change what you do under RI 2.10A?
questions.work: RI 2.10A routes by three bands: ≤60 mg/dL treat for hypoglycemia, 60–249 mg/dL recheck only if the condition changes, ≥250 mg/dL the hyperglycemia row (normal saline 500 mL if dehydrated without CHF, then 150 mL/hr).

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 2.10 Adult Diabetic Emergencies

choices.rationale: The range this question used to teach, and nothing publishes it. NIDDK puts normal fasting at 99 mg/dL or below, so 120 sits above the normal ceiling, and the 70 floor appears in no federal or RI document. It is also the wrong kind of number — a range you do nothing about.
The hypoglycemia band is right and it is half the answer. RI 2.10A has a second action band at 250 mg/dL and above, where a dehydrated patient without CHF gets a 500 mL saline bolus.

These are the two thresholds that change care. Below 60 you treat — oral glucose if the patient is awake and alert, glucagon or D10 if not. At 250 and above you move to the hyperglycemia row. Everything between is recheck-only if the condition changes.

200 mg/dL is real but it is a diagnostic threshold — NIDDK uses it for a random glucose that, with symptoms, diagnoses diabetes. It is a laboratory number, not a field action point, and RI acts at 250.

questions.note: The "70–120 mg/dL normal nonfasting range" taught in many AEMT texts has no federal or state source behind it. NIDDK publishes diagnostic thresholds rather than a field range — fasting 99 mg/dL or below is normal, 100–125 prediabetes, 126 or above diabetes — and for a random nonfasting glucose it gives no normal value at all, only 200 mg/dL or above as diagnostic. RI names no normal band either. Learn the numbers that change care.

questions.stem: Type 1 vs type 2 diabetes: which patient can still make some of their own insulin?
questions.work: The pancreas still produces insulin in type 2 (the body is resistant to it); type 1 makes none and is always insulin-dependent

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 21: Endocrine and Hematologic Emergencies (lecture slides)

choices.rationale: Reversed. Type 1 is an autoimmune destruction of the insulin-producing cells, which is why it needs insulin from diagnosis onward.
Type 1 can have a brief honeymoon with some residual production, which makes this tempting — but the defining feature is that the capacity is being destroyed, not resisted.

choices.text: Neither — both are insulin-dependent by definition
choices.rationale: Many type 2 patients do end up on insulin, which is where this comes from. Needing insulin as treatment is not the same as being unable to make it.
Type 2. The pancreas still produces insulin and the body resists it. Type 1 makes none at all and is always insulin-dependent.
